articles.text: The cattlemen of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations have been working hard to remove their cattle and now the President's order has been almost carried out. The number of cattle on the reservations was greatly overestimated. We doubt if there were any over 150,000 on the disputed ground. They have been driven in all directions, the bulk being driven into Texas.
articles.summary: Cattle have nearly all been removed from the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations under the President's order, mostly driven into Texas.

articles.text: A call for the annual meeting of the National Cattle growers' association at Chicago has been issued. It takes place in the Exposition building Nov. 17 and 18. This is the third annual meeting. Cattle raising in all its branches will be discussed by such men as Commissoner Norman, J. Coleman, Judge Carey, Gen. McPherson, Senator Cullum, A. A. Libby, Prof, Salmon, Abram, Hewitt, Col. Harris and others.

articles.text: A gambling spirit seems to be second nature to all cattlemen. Not that they are gamblers in the common sense of the word, for probably not one in ten ever gambles literally. It is their willingness to take chances to which we allude. For instance, several times lately we have heard of offers being refused on cattle on the range, which would net a larger sum than the gross Chicago price. There is a chance, though, that the price will raise by the time the cattle strike a market and the cowman is willing to take chances. We think it is an actual fact that it would be impossible to buy any large number of prime range cattle at Chicago prices, deducting freight and commission expenses.
articles.summary: Editorial on the gambling spirit of cattlemen who refuse offers above Chicago prices.

articles.text: The editor of the Glendive Times comes back at us in his last issue by almost entirely begging the question and misconstruing an expression we used in our first article about the poor ranges in eastern Montana accounting for the low prices of cattle on the Chicago market. He makes us use the expression as applying to the low price all cattle are bringing there, when to the most careless reader, it is manifest that we meant it to apply only to the cattle from the poor ranges. As well exactly might he apply the expression to the price of cattle from Australia or Patagonia as to apply it to any cattle foreign to the very ranges in question. Our article has been widely commented on, but in no instance has such a far-fetched construction been placed on our words. We are glad however, to see that the editor of the Times is beginning to acknowledge the corn by admitting that the ranges have been damaged slightly, when in his former issue he claimed that they never were better. We did not in any way wish to speak ill of the eastern Montana ranges in our first article, to the advantage of our Bad Lands ranges. We wished simply to state facts and have done so. Montana ranges are too well and favorably known to be permanently let alone because of one season's attack of drought and grasshoppers combined. That very many of those ranges are ruined for this year remains as much a fact as ever. Neither do we wish to exalt our Bad Lands ranges. They are known by all to be the very best in the country, but it is equally well known that they are nearly stocked to their full capacity allowing for the increase of the present herds. In a year or two they will be full and no advantage can be gained by either praising or condemning them in comparison with other ranges.
articles.summary: Packard answers the Glendive Times over his remarks on poor eastern Montana ranges and defends the Bad Lands ranges as nearly fully stocked.

articles.headline: Little Missouri River Stockgrowers Association Meeting.
articles.text:
The third semi-annual meeting of the Little Missouri river stockgrowers' association, met for the regular fall meeting in Roberts & Co's. old hall, last Saturday morning.

The meeting was called to order at ten o'clock by the president, Theodore Roosevelt.

Nearly all members were present or represented. The reading of the minutes of last meeting was omitted.

It being the regular meeting for the election of officers, the president advanced many cogent reasons for the election to the chair of some resident member and against his own re-election, whereupon he was immediately and unanimously re-elected president for the ensuing year.

On motion, Henry Boice was unanimously re-elected vice-president and J. L. Truscott, secretary.

On motion, it was resolved that in the absence of the president and vice-president, the secretary be empowered to call a meeting.

J. L. Truscott moved that a committee of three be appointed to consider questions relating to the fall round-up. Carried, with an amendment by Willis Eaton that the association adjourn for half an hour, pending the report of the committee. The chair appointed Chas. Rowe, Willis Eaton and H. B. Wadsworth as the round-up committee.

The meeting being again called to order by the president, the report of the round-up committee was read by Willis Eaton.

The report recommended that Jos. McCoul be appointed foreman and that the round-up date and route be as follows: Beginning at Medora, the last Tuesday, the 29th, of September, to work thence, to and one day below the mouth of Big Beaver. Thence up Big Beaver to its source, thence across to the mouth of Little Beaver, thence down the Little Missouri to Medora. The committee recommended also that the foreman receive five dollars per day salary. The report was unanimously adopted.

The chair and Willis Eaton nominated Benjamin F. Lamb as a member of the association. Mr. Lamb was unanimously elected.

The chair stated that at the spring round-up, nine mavericks were found and sold for $213.

The chair, speaking as a member of the association stated that in view of his excellent services as foreman of the spring round-up, he thought a present should be made by the association to Wal. Osterhaut.

On motion, $100 of the maverick money, was set apart, to be given to Mr. Osterhaut.

There having been reports on the river that Gregor Lang had illegally branded an animal, he explained to the satisfaction of all, that his action was entirely lawful.

Willis Eaton moved that the chair have authority to call the spring meeting a few days before the Montana association meeting at Miles City.

H. B. Wadsworth moved that the foreman be paid from any money in the treasurer's hands and that any deficit be made up at the next meeting. Carried.

Association adjourned on motion of Wm. Merrifield.
articles.summary: Minutes of the association's fall meeting, at which Theodore Roosevelt was re-elected president over his own objection and the fall round-up was set to begin at Medora Sept. 29.

articles.headline: ASSOCIATION NOTES.
articles.text: Fall round-up begins September 29.
articles.summary: The fall round-up begins September 29.

articles.text: The association can congratulate itself on again electing Theodore Roosevelt as president. Under his administration, everything moves quickly forward and there is none of that time-consuming, fruitless talk that so invariably characterizes a deliberative assembly without a good presiding officer.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy congratulates the association on re-electing Theodore Roosevelt, praising his brisk presiding.

articles.text: Chas. Rowe, of Mingusville, attended the meeting.
articles.summary: Chas. Rowe of Mingusville attended the meeting.

articles.text: John W. Buster represented the Hashknife outfit.
articles.summary: John W. Buster represented the Hashknife outfit.

articles.text: One of the most commendable things about the convention was the granting of an opportunity to Gregor Lang, to clear himself of the charge of illegally branding an animal. As was explained, he acted only as he should. We think every such charge should invariably be brought to the attention of the association. If the charge is unfounded, as it will nine times out of ten prove to be, the accused should be given the opportunity every honest man covets, of proving himself innocent. If the charge is proved true, it is for the interest of the association to find it out and punish the offender to the full extent of the law. We have heard several reports, all probably as unfounded as the one against Mr. Lang, which it would be for the interest of all concerned to have explained.
articles.summary: The paper commends the association for letting Gregor Lang clear himself of an illegal-branding charge.

articles.text: The motion to pay the foreman of the round-up good wages from the association treasury, passed unanimously, as it should. Good wages will call for and inspire good and faithful work and the fact that the foreman is receiving his pay from the association and not from an individual, will infuse a fairness into his decisions, not as likely to be found otherwise.
articles.summary: The paper approves paying the round-up foreman good wages from the association treasury.

articles.text: The combined receipts of cattle at Chicago, New York, Kansas City and St. Louis last week were 72,646, against 79,916 for the previous week. Prices during last week were very unsettled; ruling from 15 @ 30 c. lower for Texan and Western cattle. The Liverpool, England market is steady at 14 c. ℔ lb dressed for best American steers. A year ago best native cattle sold in Chicago as high as $7.50 and Texas cattle at $4.50 @ 5. During last week in Chicago, 42,000 cattle were received, making 137,969 for the past three weeks. Of the 42,000 last week about 32,900 were Texas and western cattle. Dakota range cattle touched the highest notch, Towers & Gudgell receiving $5.25. Top price for Wyoming was $5.10; for Oregon $5 and for Montana $4.40. Lowest price for western cattle was $3.25 and for Texans $2.80. Day before yesterday the market advanced 10 @ 15 c.
articles.summary: Cattle receipts and prices at Chicago and other markets; Dakota range cattle of Towers & Gudgell brought the top price of $5.25.

articles.headline: Colorado Stock Brands.
articles.text: The 12,000 or more stock brands now on file in the secretary of state's office, afford an interesting field of study. The display of ingenuity in the matter of forming combinations is remarkable. The number of combinations upon any one letter is surprising. There are, for instance, over 250 on the letter H; 150 or more on both C and D; no less than 100 each on B E, and so on through the alphabet. In making up the brand index book Mr. Edward Hanley, assistant secretary of state, says the Denver Times, has displayed excellent judgment. The brands are twice indexed; once by the names of the owners and again by brands. The latter index is the one which is to be printed and filed with the county clerks of the State. It is a very elaborate affair. The brands are arranged alphabetically or numerically, as far as practicable. There are, however, combinations on the letter, I. The letter O, the cipher, the circle, the half-circle and quarter-circle are also confusing. They are all indexed under the letter O. There will be of the 12,000 brands filed, more than 500 of each of these combinations. Those brands which cannot be classed either as letters or numerals are indexed as miscellaneous. There will probably be 1,000 of these. A large proportion of these are figures which have not been named and are as unnamable as the hieroglyphics on the pyramids of Egypt. But there are others that represent articles in common use, animals, birds, etc. The whole forms an exceedingly curious selection. The artists who have sent in these certificates have usually taken the precaution to label their representations of the various characters; a wise and thoughtful act on their part, as it would in many cases, have proven worse than a Chinese puzzle to attempt to classify them. Here are a few of the character brands: Moccasin track, turkey track, crow's feet, anchor, trowel, flags crossed, spear, table forks and pitch forks of all sorts and shapes, staples, compass, boot, shoe, cup, canteen, dipper, scissors, spades in endless variety, cow's head, jar, cannon, anvil, saddle bags, fish, hat, key, key-no, nippers, pick, hatchet boat, wineglass, horse, bull-ring, pistol, lamp, lamp chimney, arrow, swan, goose, etc., etc. The task of indexing the brands will prove an exceedingly long and tedious one. Owing to the nature of the work upon it at a time, and allowing that he works Sundays, holidays and every day, it will require nearly three months to complete the work.—[Pueblo Chieftain.
articles.summary: Clipping from the Pueblo Chieftain on the indexing of 12,000 Colorado stock brands.

articles.text: Frank Conly passed through Medora on the train Monday evening, with an alleged horse thief. He is accused of stealing thirteen head of horses but the man himself says that the horses were given to him to sell. That he sold them at public auction in Miles City but afterwards lost the money and started east. If his story does prove true, it should still go hard with him, for he was undoubtedly trying to get away from the country.

articles.text: What a sermon could be preached on the sentence used by "A Tenderfoot" in the article in last week's COW BOY, republished from the Inter Ocean: "A big white hat and a pair of spurs have made a fool of many a good boy." Add to these two a six-shooter and you have the history of four-fifths of the "ba-a-ad men." There is no westerner but has seen this very transformation. Take an eastern boy of sixteen, who at home would grow up into a good citizen, and put him in a frontier town. It actually seems that in the majority of cases, he has scarcely had time to get off the cars before he begins "packing" a six-shooter. What in the world he does it for, the poor fool himself cannot answer. As a protection, it is trebly useless. In the first place, if he conducts himself as he should, there is far less danger of getting into trouble in the west than there is in the east. In the second place, the very fact of his wearing a six-shooter gives him a "ba-a-ad" kind of feeling that will surely get him into trouble at some time and then it usually means business, for no westerner will take any chances with a man who "packs a gun." This is the most accommodating country in the world for a man who is spoiling for a fight to have his wishes gratified. But the would-be bad man and most of all, the irresponsible "kid" who thinks he must make a "gun play" to gain any reputation, receive greetings that generally paralyze them for a time. In the third place the six-shooter is worse than useless as a protection for the chances are that if he attempts to draw on a man in this country, before he can get his revolver out of the scabbard, he will be filled so full of lead that "some tenderfoot will locate him for a mineral claim." And now boys, just stop and think of the matter a moment. Not only the tenderfoot but all who make a practice of wearing six-shooters. What occasion has any one of you ever had to use a revolver in town? While a cowboy is on the range, there is some excuse for it, but how has the wearing of a six-shooter in town benefitted any one of you? On the other hand, how many instances do each one of you know where the carrying of one has lead to serious results? A little reflection on this subject by the elder heads may be of incalculable benefit to the younger ones.
articles.summary: Editorial urging young men, especially tenderfeet, to stop wearing six-shooters in town.

articles.summary: Dick Moore and Frank Miller, indicted for Luffsey's killing, cannot be found; the trial is set for the tenth.

articles.text: Seven Hashknife cowboys who have just come through from Texas with 3,000 cattle, under the foremanship of W. D. McFarlane, started home from here yesterday morning. The through cattle are in splendid condition and have been turned out on the Little Missouri Hashknife range.
articles.summary: Seven Hashknife cowboys who drove 3,000 cattle from Texas under W. D. McFarlane started home.

articles.text: Those who have not improved the opportunity of gathering plums for winter consumption, had better do so at once. No finer fruit grows than the common wild plums with which the Bad Lands abound this year. The slight frosts we have had are rapidly ripening them and they will soon be gone.
articles.summary: Wild plums abound in the Bad Lands and are ripening after slight frosts.

articles.text: Wadsworth's cavayard was coming into town Tuesday morning when Heinze was surveying the scene of the killing of Luffsey and the cowboys took Heinze for a photographer. They all began posing, and when Heinze had tired them out pointing his transit at them, he turned them loose. In the words of the immortal poet: "he never touched 'em."
articles.summary: Wadsworth's cowboys mistook surveyor Heinze for a photographer and posed for him.

articles.text: It would be a good idea for some people to receive exactly the kind of treatment they give their stock and see if it would sharpen their feelings any. We have seen one team especially driven into town early in the morning and allowed to stand all day long and sometimes far into the night, without a bite to eat or a drop to drink. If this had happened once only, it might be excusable, but happening time after time makes the matter not only a subject for public comment but for public action, if this shameful mal-treatment continues.
articles.summary: Editorial against leaving teams standing all day in town without food or water.

articles.text: The article in our last issue about the chronic borrower has, we think, received more favorable comment from our readers here, than any article that has ever appeared in the COW BOY. Of course there are times when a person is compelled to borrow, but they are exceptional circumstances. The point of borrowing reducing the circulating medium in a town and thereby proving a detriment did not receive due attention. The borrower is a non-producer to just the extent of his borrowing and to the same extent damages the town, for if he had bought or rented what he borrowed, he would have put into circulation just that much money. By his borrowing also, he actually takes away from the circulating medium by keeping back value for value received. Even when a person realizes the true spirit of the chronic borrower it is very hard to refuse the loan of some article which is asked. One scarcely likes to tell him that he can hire or buy the same article right here and for this very reason the chronic borrower has a rich field to work and the man who provides himself with the articles he needs is thus a constant prey to the one who is either too stingy to buy what he needs or wants to indulge himself in luxuries beyond his means. We doubt even now if our article will cause any refusal of loans but we already know of several instances where it has kept people from borrowing articles. It is an unpopular plan with some to champion the anti-borrower cause, but we have enlisted for the war now and propose to keep hammering on this subject just as often as we see it will do any good.
articles.summary: Editorial continuing the Cow Boy's campaign against the chronic borrower.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt re-elected president of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association
events.summary: At the association's fall meeting in Roberts & Co.'s old hall, Roosevelt presided, argued for electing a resident member instead of himself, and was immediately and unanimously re-elected. Henry Boice was re-elected vice-president and J. L. Truscott secretary.
events.excerpt: the president advanced many cogent reasons for the election to the chair of some resident member and against his own re-election, whereupon he was immediately and unanimously re-elected

events.date_basis: "the last Tuesday, the 29th, of September" per round-up committee report
events.title: Fall round-up set to begin at Medora under foreman Jos. McCoul
events.summary: The association adopted its committee's report naming Jos. McCoul foreman at five dollars a day and setting the route from Medora down to below the mouth of Big Beaver, up Big Beaver, across to Little Beaver and back down the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Beginning at Medora, the last Tuesday, the 29th, of September, to work thence, to and one day below the mouth of Big Beaver.

events.date_basis: meeting "last Saturday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Association rewards spring round-up foreman Wal. Osterhaut from maverick money
events.summary: The chairman reported that nine mavericks found at the spring round-up sold for $213. Roosevelt, speaking as a member, proposed a present for foreman Wal. Osterhaut, and $100 of the maverick money was set apart for him.
events.excerpt: The chair stated that at the spring round-up, nine mavericks were found and sold for $213.

events.date_basis: meeting "last Saturday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Gregor Lang clears himself of illegal-branding charge before the association
events.summary: Lang explained to the association's satisfaction that his branding of an animal was lawful, and the Cow Boy commended the association for giving him the chance.
events.excerpt: he explained to the satisfaction of all, that his action was entirely lawful.

events.date_basis: meeting "last Saturday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Benjamin F. Lamb elected to the stockgrowers' association
events.summary: On nomination by the chair (Roosevelt) and Willis Eaton, Benjamin F. Lamb was unanimously elected a member; the meeting adjourned on motion of Wm. Merrifield.
events.excerpt: The chair and Willis Eaton nominated Benjamin F. Lamb as a member of the association.

events.date_basis: editorial comment in issue of Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Cow Boy praises Roosevelt's handling of the association
events.summary: The paper congratulated the association on again electing Roosevelt, saying that under him business moves quickly without fruitless talk.
events.excerpt: The association can congratulate itself on again electing Theodore Roosevelt as president.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: W. W. Sewall of the Elk Horn Ranch registers at the Northern Pacific hotel
events.summary: The weekly hotel list named W. W. Sewall of the Elk Horn Ranch among arrivals at Medora's Northern Pacific hotel, along with Hashknife men and visitors from Chicago, New York and Holland.
events.excerpt: W W Sewall, Elk Horn Ranch

events.date_basis: "last Monday morning" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Sixteen witnesses leave Medora for the de Morès trial at Bismarck
events.summary: Sixteen persons subpoenaed in Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock, Dick Moore and Frank Miller left Medora for Bismarck.
events.excerpt: Sixteen persons were subpœnaed as witnesses in the case of the Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock, Dick Moore and Frank Miller

events.date_basis: trial "set for the tenth"; issue of Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: De Morès trial for the killing of Luffsey set to open
events.summary: The trial for the killing of Luffsey was set for the tenth. Co-defendants Dick Moore and Frank Miller could not be found, and visitors to Bismarck expected an acquittal.
events.excerpt: Their whereabouts is at present unknown, and it is doubtful if they will be present at the trial, which is set for the tenth.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Surveyor Paul Heinze maps the scene of the Luffsey shooting
events.summary: Paul Heinze of Bismarck surveyed the scene of the shooting in which Luffsey was killed, for submission to the jury; Wadsworth's cowboys, driving in their cavayard, took him for a photographer and posed.
events.excerpt: surveying the scene of the shooting affray in which Luffsey was killed. His survey will be submitted to the jury.

events.date_basis: "Sunday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Luffsey case witness McNeavo Nally returns to Medora
events.summary: McNeavo Nally, a former Medora resident now at Jamestown and a witness in the Luffsey murder case, came in with surveyor Heinze.
events.excerpt: He is a witness in the Luffsey murder case and accompanied surveyor Heinze here.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: De Morès case moved to Bismarck on change of venue
events.summary: A syndicated Dakota news item reported that the case of the "Marquis de Moses" had been removed to Bismarck on a change of venue granted by Judge Francis.
events.excerpt: The case of the Marquis de Moses has been removed to Bismarck, on a change of venue granted by Judge Francis.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: The Marquise pays the Medora teacher's salary
events.summary: The Marquise donated the teacher's salary, leaving the school board to raise only the other expenses for the winter.
events.excerpt: The Marquise has generously donated the teacher's salary and the school board will only have to rustle for the other expenses.

events.date_basis: "last Sunday morning" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Murphy Bros. complete cattle contract with the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.
events.summary: Five hundred bar-brand cattle averaging 1089½ pounds were delivered to the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., completing the Murphy Bros. contract of 2,500 head; Mat. and Billy Murphy left for the west Monday.
events.excerpt: Last Sunday's delivery completed the Murphy Bros. contract with the Co. 2,500 head have been delivered averaging a little over 1090.

events.date_basis: "yesterday morning" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Hashknife cowboys head home after driving 3,000 Texas cattle to the Little Missouri
events.summary: Seven Hashknife cowboys who brought 3,000 cattle up from Texas under foreman W. D. McFarlane started home from Medora; the cattle were turned out on the Hashknife range.
events.excerpt: Seven Hashknife cowboys who have just come through from Texas with 3,000 cattle, under the foremanship of W. D. McFarlane, started home from here yesterday morning.

events.date_basis: "last night" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Dr. Jorgens returns from Spearfish with news of a burned stage station
events.summary: Dr. Jorgens and family returned from Spearfish. He reported the North Grand stage station burned, Aleck Connel's purchase of Gallup & Walton's Cave Hills ranch, and the E6 outfit's beef round-up.
events.excerpt: Dr. Jorgens reports that the North Grand stage station is burned.

events.date_basis: "Monday evening" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Alleged horse thief taken through Medora
events.summary: Frank Conly passed through on the train with a man accused of stealing thirteen horses, who claimed he had sold them at auction in Miles City for their owner.
events.excerpt: Frank Conly passed through Medora on the train Monday evening, with an alleged horse thief.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Cowboys tried at Miles City for delaying train at Mingusville
events.summary: The cowboys who delayed the train at Mingusville and tried to make Conductor Clark dance were being tried at Miles City.
events.excerpt: The case of the cowboys who delayed the train at Mingusville and amused themselves by trying to make Conductor Clark dance, is now being tried at Miles City.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Railroad reserves Mingusville land for cattle shippers
events.summary: The railroad company took the land about Mingusville off the market to reserve it as grazing ground for cattle shippers.
events.excerpt: The whole will be reserved for grazing grounds for cattle shippers.

events.date_basis: "this morning", issue of Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Slaughter-house finished; John McGee leaves for Jamestown
events.summary: John McGee left for Jamestown after completing the finishing touches on the slaughter-house, which was called second to none in the United States except in size.
events.excerpt: John McGee left this morning for Jimtown, having concluded the finishing touches on the slaughter-house.

events.date_basis: "this morning", issue of Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Birdie Wadsworth leaves for school in Bismarck
events.summary: Miss Birdie Wadsworth started for Bismarck to attend school for the winter.
events.excerpt: Miss Birdie Wadsworth started for Bismarck this morning, where she will attend school this winter.

events.date_basis: "last night" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Henry Harmon of Mandan visits
events.summary: Henry Harmon of Mandan made a flying visit and returned home the next morning.
events.excerpt: Henry Harmon of Mandan, made us a flying visit last night.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: B. Barr in Medora to buy cattle for the 777 outfit's Berthold contract
events.summary: B. Barr remained in Medora and was expected to buy cattle for the Berthold contract of the 777 outfit.
events.excerpt: He will probably buy the cattle for the Berthold contract of the 777 outfit.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: C. VanEeghen at the Garner creek horse ranch
events.summary: C. VanEeghen, brother of J. A. VanEeghen, was at the Garner creek horse ranch.
events.excerpt: C. VanEeghen, brother of J. A., is at the Garner creek horse ranch.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Alex. Morton of South Heart in town
events.summary: Alex. Morton of South Heart, brother of Dr. Morton, was in Medora.
events.excerpt: Alex. Morton of South Heart, brother of Dr. Morton, was in town Tuesday.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Howard Eaton and Link Gates kill mountain sheep
events.summary: Several mountain sheep had been killed lately, most recently by Howard Eaton and Link. Gates.
events.excerpt: Several mountain sheep have been killed lately, the last lucky hunters being Howard Eaton and Link. Gates.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: "Rustler" Marney of the Stockgrowers Journal visits the Cow Boy
events.summary: Marney of the Stockgrowers Journal called at the Cow Boy office.
events.excerpt: "Rustler" Marney, of the Stockgrowers Journal, made us a visit Monday.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Gill Kennedy moves building to open an oyster restaurant
events.summary: Gill Kennedy moved his building across the river to the lot where John Warn's restaurant stood and planned a restaurant dealing mainly in oysters.
events.excerpt: He intends opening up a restaurant, dealing principally in oysters.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Wild plums ripen in the Bad Lands after slight frosts
events.summary: The paper urged readers to gather the abundant wild plums, which slight frosts were rapidly ripening.
events.excerpt: No finer fruit grows than the common wild plums with which the Bad Lands abound this year.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Packard receives a Webster's Unabridged Dictionary
events.summary: The Cow Boy received a Webster's Unabridged Dictionary from the publishers through J. W. Clarke of Bismarck, which Packard credited to his "Cowboy Dictionary."
events.excerpt: we suppose it is due to our "Cowboy Dictionary."

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Cow Boy disputes the Glendive Times over eastern Montana ranges
events.summary: Packard answered the Glendive Times, saying drought and grasshoppers had ruined many eastern Montana ranges for the year and that the Bad Lands ranges were nearly fully stocked.
events.excerpt: That very many of those ranges are ruined for this year remains as much a fact as ever.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Dakota range cattle top the Chicago market
events.summary: Towers & Gudgell's Dakota range cattle brought the week's top western price at Chicago, $5.25.
events.excerpt: Dakota range cattle touched the highest notch, Towers & Gudgell receiving $5.25.

events.date_basis: "About April 15" in strayed notice
events.title: Howard Eaton's bay gelding strays
events.summary: Howard Eaton advertised for a four-year-old bay gelding branded on the shoulder and hip, lost about April 15 wearing a hackamore.
events.excerpt: About April 15, a bay gelding four years old, branded pickaxe s, on left shoulder and VI on left hip.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Packard offers cattle and outfit for sale
events.summary: A. T. Packard advertised cows, steers, heifers and bulls from Minnesota and Iowa, with horses and outfit if desired.
events.excerpt: The stock is all in good condition and is from Minnesota and Iowa.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 10 Sep 1885
events.title: Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations cleared of cattle
events.summary: The paper reported the President's order to remove cattle from the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations almost carried out, the herds driven mostly into Texas.
events.excerpt: They have been driven in all directions, the bulk being driven into Texas.
